overview.title: Chapter 16 summary (part 2): reliability, fine-tuning, memory, LoRA, modalities
overview.main_topic: The second half of the chapter 16 summary: hallucination, instruction fine-tuning (supervised and RL-based), accelerator memory as the bottleneck, LoRA, multimodal LLMs and foundation models
overview.central_idea: Pretrained LLMs are unreliable and hallucinate; instruction fine-tuning (from simple instruction/response training to RL) turns them into chat assistants; memory is the main practical constraint, which LoRA addresses by training only a low-rank update to attention projections; and the same sequence-prediction recipe extends to other modalities, giving rise to the broader notion of foundation models.
overview.importance: These six bullets compress sections 16.3 and 16.4 (p.508–528). Each is a checkpoint: if you cannot explain one, return to the cited pages.
learning_objectives: Explain why hallucination is a fundamental property of LLMs rather than an occasional bug
Distinguish supervised instruction fine-tuning from RL-based instruction fine-tuning
Explain why accelerator memory, not compute throughput, is usually the bottleneck when training LLMs
Describe how LoRA reduces trainable parameters and memory, and compute its parameter savings
Explain how multimodal inputs/outputs are framed as sequence prediction
prerequisites: Memory use of the Adam optimizer and LoRA (p.514–517)

summary:
This page completes the chapter 16 summary started on p.530 and then ends the chapter.

- **LLM output is unreliable**: every LLM will sometimes hallucinate factually incorrect information (p.494, p.512).
- **Instruction fine-tuning** adapts an LLM to follow instructions in a chat dialog. The simplest form trains directly on instruction/response pairs with the ordinary next-token loss (*supervised fine-tuning*, p.512, p.519); more advanced forms use **reinforcement learning** (RLHF, p.519; RL for reasoning, p.527–528).
- **Accelerator memory** is the most common resource bottleneck: weights, gradients and optimizer state must all fit on the GPU/TPU (p.514).
- **LoRA** reduces memory by freezing most Transformer parameters and only training a *low-rank decomposition* added to the attention projection weights (p.515–516). With rank 8 on a 2048×2048 kernel, 32,768 trainable parameters replace 4,194,304.
- **Multimodality**: LLMs can take in or produce images, audio and other data if you can frame those inputs/outputs as sequences in a sequence-prediction problem (p.522–524).
- **Foundation model** is the general term for models of any modality trained with self-supervision on broad data and usable for many downstream tasks (p.525).

The rest of the page is blank; chapter 17 (image generation) begins on p.532 and picks up the foundation-model theme with diffusion models.

paragraphs.excerpt: LLM output is unreliable, and all LLMs will occasionally hallucinate factually incorrect information.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Summary bullet: LLM outputs cannot be fully trusted; all LLMs sometimes produce factually wrong statements (hallucinations).
paragraphs.what_it_means: An LLM is trained to produce *likely* continuations, not *true* ones. When the most likely-sounding continuation is false — for instance, a confident answer about something the model never saw — it produces it anyway, with no signal that it is wrong. The word 'all' is deliberate: it is a property of the approach, not of a particular model.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Any application built on LLMs needs verification, retrieval (RAG, p.525) or human oversight where correctness matters.

terminology.meaning: Fluent output that is factually incorrect or unsupported, produced without any indication of uncertainty.

connections: p.494: GPT-3's output can 'veer from accurate to completely false with zero indication'.
p.512: 'Hallucinations and uncontrollable output are fundamental problems with language models.'
p.525: retrieval augmented generation grounds answers in retrieved documents to reduce this.

paragraphs.excerpt: LLMs can be fine-tuned to follow instructions in a chat dialog. This type of
paragraphs.what_it_says: Summary bullet: fine-tuning an LLM to follow instructions in a chat is called instruction fine-tuning. The simplest form trains directly on instruction and response pairs; more advanced forms involve reinforcement learning. (The bullet continues in elements e05–e07.)
paragraphs.what_it_means: A pretrained model only autocompletes text. Supervised instruction fine-tuning concatenates a prompt and a desired response (with consistent markers like "[instruction]" and "[response]", p.512) and trains with the same next-token loss, nudging the model toward assistant-like answers. RL-based methods go further: instead of imitating fixed answers, the model is rewarded for outputs a reward model (RLHF) or an automatic checker prefers.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the step that turns a base model like the pretrained Gemma into a usable chatbot.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Supervised fine-tuning = maximum likelihood on curated pairs; RL fine-tuning = maximizing an expected reward over the model's own samples.

terminology.meaning: Further training of a pretrained LLM so it responds to user instructions in a dialog.
The book's name (p.519) for instruction fine-tuning on hand-curated prompt/response pairs.
Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback: a reward model trained from human preference rankings guides further training (p.519).

connections: p.512–513: instruction fine-tuning Gemma on the Databricks dolly dataset.
p.519: RLHF and the term supervised fine-tuning.
p.527–528: RL with verifiable answers for reasoning models.

paragraphs.excerpt: The most common resource bottleneck when working with LLMs is accelerator memory.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Summary bullet: the main practical limit when working with LLMs is the memory of the GPU/TPU.
paragraphs.what_it_means: During training each parameter needs storage for itself, its gradient and the optimizer state, plus activations for the backward pass. For the 1B-parameter Gemma, weights take about 3.7 GB, and with Adam the weights plus optimizer state reach about 15 GB — leaving no room on a 16 GB Colab GPU (p.514). So whether you can train at all depends on memory, not on how fast the chip computes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It motivates parameter-efficient methods (LoRA), lower precision, and the multi-device techniques of chapter 18.

terminology.meaning: The on-device memory (VRAM/HBM) of a GPU or TPU, which must hold model weights, optimizer state and activations.

connections: p.514: the out-of-memory problem when calling fit() on Gemma with Adam.
p.508: training across multiple machines is deferred to chapter 18.

paragraphs.excerpt: LoRA is a technique to reduce memory usage by freezing most Transformer parameters
paragraphs.what_it_says: Summary bullet: LoRA saves memory by freezing most Transformer parameters and updating only a low-rank decomposition of the attention projection weights.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Instead of training a full $d\times d$ kernel, LoRA keeps it frozen and adds a product of two thin matrices, `alpha` ($d\times r$) and `beta` ($r\times d$), whose output is added to the frozen projection (p.515). Frozen parameters need no gradients or optimizer state, so memory drops sharply. The book applies it with `enable_lora(rank=8)` to the query and key projections of every attention layer.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It made fine-tuning Gemma possible on a single 16 GB GPU, and the same idea is widely used to adapt large models cheaply.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Low rank works because fine-tuning needs much less expressive power than pretraining (p.515); the update matrix is assumed to live in a small subspace.

terminology.meaning: Writing a matrix as the product of two smaller matrices through a narrow inner dimension r (the rank).
The query, key and value (and output) Dense kernels inside multi-head attention.

connections: p.515: Linear vs. LoraLinear layers and the 4,194,304 vs. 32,768 parameter comparison.
p.516: figure 16.4 and manually enabling LoRA on key_dense and query_dense.
p.288–289: freezing layers during fine-tuning in chapter 8 — the same idea, at layer granularity.

paragraphs.excerpt: LLMs can input or output data from different modalities if you can figure out
paragraphs.what_it_says: Summary bullet: LLMs can handle other modalities (images, audio, …) as input or output if those can be framed as sequences in a sequence prediction problem.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The Transformer doesn't care what a token represents. Turn an image into a sequence of patch embeddings, or audio into a sequence of codes, and the same next-token machinery applies. The hard part is the framing — choosing how to tokenize or embed the new modality.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains how today's vision-language models work and why the line between 'language model' and general sequence model is blurring.

terminology.meaning: A type of data, such as text, images, audio or video.

connections: p.525: the 'large language model' name becomes misleading as models handle images and audio.

paragraphs.excerpt: A foundation model is a general term for models of any modality trained
paragraphs.what_it_says: Summary bullet: 'foundation model' is the general term for models of any modality trained with self-supervision for a wide range of downstream tasks.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The defining properties are a self-supervised (reconstruction) objective on broad, internet-scale data and general-purpose use via fine-tuning or prompting, not a specific architecture. LLMs are the best-known example, but diffusion image models (chapter 17) are foundation models too.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It bridges to chapter 17, which starts on the next page with image generation and diffusion models.

terminology.meaning: A model trained on broad data with self-supervision at scale that can be adapted to many downstream tasks (p.525).
A specific application (classification, chat, captioning…) that a pretrained model is adapted to.

connections: p.525: full definition of foundation models.
p.532: chapter 17 begins, covering diffusion models, which the book calls another kind of internet-scale self-supervised model.

concepts.name: Hallucination
concepts.definition: Confident, fluent generation of incorrect information by an LLM.
concepts.intuition: The model is an expert at sounding right, not at being right.
concepts.technical: Next-token likelihood training rewards plausible continuations; nothing in the objective checks facts.
concepts.significance: A fundamental limit of LLMs that applications must design around.
concepts.example: Gemma producing a nonsensical completion on p.512 because it couldn't find a more likely continuation.
concepts.misconception: That a sufficiently large model stops hallucinating — the book says all LLMs occasionally do.

concepts.name: Instruction fine-tuning
concepts.definition: Additional training that makes a pretrained LLM follow user instructions in a dialog.
concepts.intuition: Teaching an autocomplete engine to behave like an assistant by showing it examples of good answers.
concepts.technical: Simplest form: next-token loss on concatenated instruction/response sequences (supervised). Advanced: reinforcement learning (e.g., RLHF).
concepts.example: Fine-tuning Gemma on instruction/response pairs from the Databricks dataset (p.512).
concepts.misconception: That instruction tuning teaches the model new knowledge — the book says it mostly nudges an already learned representation (p.512).

concepts.name: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)
concepts.definition: Fine-tuning by freezing pretrained weights and training a low-rank additive update.
concepts.intuition: Instead of repainting the whole wall, add a thin transparent overlay that only needs a few brush strokes.
concepts.technical: Output $= xW + (xA)B$ with $W$ frozen, $A\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times r}$, $B\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{out}}$, $r\ll d$.
concepts.significance: Huge memory savings: no gradients or optimizer state for frozen weights.
concepts.example: Rank 8 on a 2048×2048 kernel: 32,768 trainable parameters instead of 4,194,304 (p.515).
concepts.misconception: That LoRA shrinks the model — the full frozen weights are still loaded; only the trainable part is small.

concepts.name: Accelerator memory bottleneck
concepts.definition: The limit imposed by GPU/TPU memory on which models can be trained or served.
concepts.intuition: It doesn't matter how fast the oven is if the dish doesn't fit inside.
concepts.technical: Training memory ≈ weights + gradients + optimizer state + activations; with Adam, the first three are several times the weight memory.
concepts.significance: Throughput is a secondary concern to fitting the model on the device (p.514).
concepts.example: 1B-parameter Gemma: ~3.7 GB of weights, ~15 GB with Adam state, on a 16 GB GPU (p.514).
concepts.misconception: That if inference fits in memory, training will too.

concepts.name: Multimodal LLM
concepts.definition: An LLM that reads or generates data from modalities other than text.
concepts.intuition: Anything you can turn into a sequence of tokens, a Transformer can learn to predict.
concepts.technical: Non-text inputs are encoded into token-like embeddings and interleaved with text tokens.
concepts.significance: Extends the LLM recipe to images, audio and more.
concepts.example: A model that takes an image plus a question and outputs a textual answer (p.522–524).
concepts.misconception: That multimodality requires a fundamentally new architecture — the key is framing data as sequences.

concepts.name: Foundation model
concepts.definition: A model of any modality trained with self-supervision on broad data and adaptable to many downstream tasks.
concepts.intuition: A general-purpose base that many specific applications are built on.
concepts.technical: Hallmarks: self-supervised reconstruction objective, internet-scale data, no single target task (p.525).
concepts.significance: Unifies LLMs and other large generative models such as diffusion models.

math.title: LoRA parameter count (behind the LoRA summary bullet)
math.source_text: frozen = ops.matmul(inputs, self.kernel); update = ops.matmul(ops.matmul(inputs, self.alpha), self.beta); return frozen + update (p.515)

variables.meaning: the LoRA rank (8 in the book)

math.operations: Two matrix products through a narrow inner dimension r, added to the frozen projection.
math.purpose: Quantifies how LoRA 'reduces memory usage' as stated in the summary.
math.interpretation: The update $AB$ is a $d_{in}\times d_{out}$ matrix of rank at most r, so it can only change W in r independent directions.
math.intuition: The whole update must squeeze through r numbers at the narrow middle point.

deeper.title: Rough memory budget for fine-tuning with and without LoRA
deeper.body:
Using the book's figures for Gemma 3 1B (p.514): weights ≈ 3.7 GB in 32-bit floats; Adam adds three more floats per trainable parameter, so full fine-tuning needs ≈ 4 × 3.7 ≈ 15 GB before activations.

With LoRA, the base weights (3.7 GB) stay in memory but have no gradients or optimizer state. If the LoRA parameters are, say, a few million (rank 8 on query and key projections across all layers), their weights plus Adam state are only tens of MB. Activations still need memory, but the total now fits on a 16 GB GPU. (Estimate of the LoRA parameter total is an AI illustration, not a figure from the book.)

deeper.title: Two flavors of instruction fine-tuning
deeper.body:
| | Supervised (simplest) | Reinforcement learning (advanced) |
|---|---|---|
| Data | Fixed instruction/response pairs | Model's own sampled responses |
| Signal | Next-token loss on the given response | Reward from a reward model (RLHF) or a checker |
| Book pages | p.512–513 | p.519–521, p.527–528 |
| Limitation | Only imitates curated answers | Needs a reliable reward |

deeper.title: Beyond the book: which projections get LoRA?
deeper.body: The book applies LoRA to the query and key projections (p.515–516) and notes you could also add it to the value projection. In the original LoRA paper's main experiments, the authors adapted the query and value projections ($W_q$, $W_v$); in practice many libraries also adapt all attention and MLP projections. The choice is a hyperparameter trading trainable parameters for adaptation capacity.

visualizations.title: LoRA trainable parameters vs. rank for a 2048×2048 kernel
visualizations.why: The LoRA bullet says only a low-rank decomposition is updated; p.515 compares a 2048×2048 kernel with a rank-8 update. This chart shows how trainable parameters grow with rank compared with the frozen kernel.

misconceptions.claim: Only small or poorly trained LLMs hallucinate.
misconceptions.correction: The summary says all LLMs will occasionally hallucinate; it follows from training on next-token likelihood rather than truth.

misconceptions.claim: Instruction fine-tuning always requires reinforcement learning.
misconceptions.correction: The simplest form is ordinary supervised training on instruction/response pairs with the next-token loss; RL is the more advanced variant.

misconceptions.claim: LoRA makes the model itself smaller.
misconceptions.correction: The frozen pretrained weights remain; LoRA reduces the number of *trainable* parameters and thus gradient and optimizer memory.

misconceptions.claim: The speed of the GPU is the main constraint on LLM fine-tuning.
misconceptions.correction: The book identifies accelerator memory as the most common bottleneck; throughput is secondary to fitting the model (p.514).

takeaways: All LLMs hallucinate occasionally; outputs need verification where correctness matters.
Instruction fine-tuning ranges from supervised training on instruction/response pairs to reinforcement learning.
Accelerator memory is the usual bottleneck: weights, gradients and optimizer state must fit on the device.
LoRA freezes the base model and trains a small low-rank update to attention projections, slashing memory.
Other modalities can be handled by framing them as sequence prediction.
Foundation models: self-supervised, broad-data models of any modality, adaptable to many tasks.

questions.question: What is the simplest form of instruction fine-tuning according to the summary?
options: Reinforcement learning with a reward model
Training directly on instruction and response pairs
Freezing the model and adding LoRA weights
Pretraining a new model on chat transcripts from scratch
questions.answer: Training directly on instruction and response pairs
questions.explanation: The summary says the simplest form trains on instruction/response pairs; RL is the more advanced form. LoRA is a memory-saving technique that can be combined with fine-tuning but is not itself a form of instruction tuning, and pretraining from scratch is not fine-tuning.

questions.question: Why is accelerator memory, rather than raw compute, usually the bottleneck when fine-tuning an LLM?
questions.answer: Training must hold weights, gradients, optimizer state (Adam adds several values per parameter) and activations on the device; for a 1B model this already reaches ~15 GB before activations, so the model may simply not fit.
questions.explanation: See the memory arithmetic on p.514; speed only matters once the model fits.

questions.question: A projection kernel has shape 4096 × 4096. How many trainable parameters does a rank-16 LoRA update have, and what fraction of the kernel's parameters is that?
questions.answer: 16 × (4096 + 4096) = 131,072 trainable parameters; the kernel has 16,777,216, so about 0.78%.
questions.explanation: alpha is 4096×16 and beta is 16×4096 (p.515). The ratio r(d_in+d_out)/(d_in d_out) = 2r/d = 32/4096 ≈ 0.0078.

questions.question: Why does freezing parameters save memory during training, beyond simply not updating them?
questions.answer: Frozen parameters need no stored gradients and no optimizer state (e.g., Adam's moment estimates), which for Adam is several times the size of the weights themselves.
questions.explanation: The book points out on p.514 that freezing saves memory because no optimizer variables are tracked for frozen parameters.

questions.question: Which statement best matches the book's definition of a foundation model?
options: Any Transformer with more than a billion parameters
A model of any modality trained with self-supervision for a wide range of downstream tasks
An LLM that has been instruction fine-tuned for chat
A model trained on labeled data for one specific task
questions.answer: A model of any modality trained with self-supervision for a wide range of downstream tasks
questions.explanation: The definition is about training objective and generality, not size or architecture; instruction tuning is a downstream adaptation; single-task supervised models are the opposite of foundation models.

questions.question: What must you figure out to make an LLM work with a new modality such as audio?
questions.answer: How to frame the audio input or output as a sequence (of tokens or embeddings) so the problem becomes sequence prediction.
questions.explanation: Directly from the multimodality bullet; the Transformer machinery stays the same.

questions.question: Without looking back, can you explain to a friend why LLMs hallucinate and name two techniques from chapter 16 that make LLM outputs more useful or controllable?
questions.answer: They optimize for likely text, not true text. Techniques: instruction fine-tuning (supervised or RLHF), retrieval augmented generation, reasoning via chain of thought.
questions.explanation: If you couldn't name the techniques, revisit p.512, p.519 and p.525–526.
